transcript:
Header: 2026-03-15 15:00 UTC | Duration: 46m | Attendees: Maya P., Leo C., Rajesh K., Elena M., Samir P.

[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick check-in, we ran the throughput tests yesterday and have some numbers to go through
[00:12] Rajesh Kumar: Yep thanks, we saw the dashboard, numbers looked good but p99 spiked a bit when concurrency hit around 300
[00:22] Leo Chen: Right, so quick context, we ran the continuous batching run with the default window of 20ms, batch sizes averaged ~22 tokens per request, and throughput peaked at 3.2k tokens/sec for the model variant you chose
[00:38] Elena Morales: 3.2k tokens/sec, but what does that mean for end-to-end rtt, our 200ms SLO was breached at higher concurrencies
[00:52] Leo Chen: Exactly, average latency stayed ~120-150ms up to 150 concurrent, once we push to 300 concurrent the queueing added ~180-240ms extra which pushed p99 to ~650ms
[01:08] Samir Patel: There was also a CPU jitter on the host level, sometimes we saw context switching, maybe due to our proxy config
[01:20] Maya Patel: Good catch, Samir. Two threads: one is infra-level tuning (proxy/threads) and second is runtime-level batching/concurrency tuning. For the latter we recommended an initial concurrency cap at 200 and a slight increase in batching window to 30ms to allow larger batches and better throughput
[01:40] Rajesh Kumar: Increasing window sounds risky for latency, will that blow up p95/p99 for small requests?
[01:50] Leo Chen: There's a tradeoff. For your workload, many requests are small (avg 80 tokens). A small bump to 30ms increases batch size without adding much per-request delay because we already buffer in the prefix cache. We've seen 10-15% token/sec gain with minimal p95 impact in similar pilots
[02:10] Elena Morales: What about KV cache effects? We rely on repeated prefixes for multi-turn chat
[02:18] Leo Chen: KV/prefix cache reduces decoder work significantly. In our logs, hits were ~62% during the run, that cut the per-token compute and pushed throughput up. If cache miss patterns change under higher concurrency we should see p99 changes though
[02:36] Rajesh Kumar: Can you explain the queueing model again? We saw queue depth spikes and wondered if that was the serving runtime or our ingress
[02:45] Leo Chen: Sure. By default requests hit the routing layer which places them into per-model queues. From there continuous batching pulls requests into the GPU runner. If the queue backs up it's usually ingress caused or concurrency limit too low; sometimes autoscaler lag can also cause transient spikes
[03:06] Samir Patel: Our ingress is Kong with a 16 worker config. We may need to tune that and also increase connection pool sizes
[03:14] Maya Patel: Action item for Samir to try 32 workers and increase pool size, please share before next run
[03:22] Rajesh Kumar: Ok
[03:28] Leo Chen: For the next benchmark we propose two runs: target concurrency 200 (baseline) and 400 (stress). We'll capture token/sec, p50/p95/p99 and queue depth histograms. We'll also enable a short-tail configuration where long-running requests are routed to a slower model variant to protect SLOs
[03:50] Elena Morales: How do you do the slow-path routing? That's critical for us, we can't have short requests suffering from long token generations
[03:58] Leo Chen: We set policy rules at the smart routing layer: if predicted seq length > X or if request hits a heavy custom tool, route to a bigger model with higher latency but more stable throughput, or to a variant with lower qps cost. Also fallback to dedicated capacity if the hosted pool is at 90% utilization
[04:20] Rajesh Kumar: Is the fallback automatic or do we need canary/rollout config?
[04:26] Maya Patel: It can be automatic with thresholds you set, we typically set a soft threshold to trigger canary first, then full fallback if canary fails
[04:35] Samir Patel: There was a question on encryption/KMS latency — our security team flagged that calling KMS for keys on every request might add overhead
[04:45] Leo Chen: Good point. We recommend caching the DEK locally for session duration to avoid per-request KMS calls. That adds very little risk when keys rotate properly. We'll document best practices in the guide
[05:00] Rajesh Kumar: Also curious on quantization effects — you shipped a 4-bit quantized model; any adverse impacts at high throughput?
[05:08] Leo Chen: 4-bit gives great memory savings and faster kernel paths, but you can see some variance in tail latency due to different kernel scheduling. We'll share kernel-level traces. For your POC the quantized variant was beneficial overall
[05:22] Elena Morales: Can we also simulate bursty traffic? Real traffic is not uniform, we have spikes to 600 qps for a few mins
[05:30] Leo Chen: Yes, we'll add a burst pattern in the 400-concurrency run; also recommend testing queueing with a leaky-bucket ingress to emulate bursts
[05:40] Maya Patel: Quick recap: Redwood runs two benchmark profiles (200 and 400 concurrency), enable 30ms batching window, collect p50/p95/p99 and queue depth hist; Fintera provides a representative production trace and tries Kong tuning; next sync we review results and decide on target reserved capacity / dedicated test
[06:00] Rajesh Kumar: Sounds good, one more question — what's the expected cost delta if we move to higher concurrency and larger batches vs raising dedicated capacity?
[06:12] Maya Patel: Short answer: batching usually reduces per-token compute so costs drop per output token, but higher concurrency can increase tail latency risking SLOs. Dedicated reserved capacity has predictable cost but you pay for idle headroom. We'll include rough cost estimates in the follow-up
[06:30] Elena Morales: Please include specific numbers, that's the team that signs off
[06:36] Leo Chen: Will do. We'll put a cost-per-1M-token estimate for each config
[06:40] Rajesh Kumar: Great, thanks
[06:45] Maya Patel: Any blockers on the timeline? We aim to run the benchmarks this week
[06:50] Elena Morales: We'll try to get the logs and traces by tomorrow EOD
[06:54] Maya Patel: Perfect, thanks everyone

[End of meeting]
